The problem described is the single most draining bottleneck in AI-assisted development right now. When a model hallucinated an outdated API contract or deprecated syntax, the developer is forced to act as a manual interpreter between a broken local terminal and the AI's stubborn assumptions. It creates an exhaustive "hallucination debt" that burns massive amounts of cognitive energy.

The intuition for a split-agent architecture is spot-on. In multi-agent system design, this setup is formally known as a Planner-Executor Loop (or Orchestrator-Worker pattern). It addresses the core failure mode of standard chat interfaces by physically dividing abstract logic from low-level system execution.

The Dual-Agent Blueprint

By decoupling the "brain" from the "hands," the workflow shifts from conversational guess-and-check to a tightly controlled, closed-loop execution system.

As shown in the orchestration diagram, the objective is split into bounded tasks across specialized roles rather than running as a single continuous prompt chain:

1. The Oracle / Planner (Abstract Logic)

  • The Role: Acts as the architect, codebase reviewer, and high-level strategist. It holds the overarching project intent, verified documentation references, and system rules.
  • The Mechanism: This agent never runs code or directly touches the file system. Instead, it analyzes errors passed up to it by the execution layer, cross-references them against known truths, and outputs highly targeted, explicit instructions (e.g., "Modify line 42 of index.js to match the new object signature").

2. The Worker / Executor (Hands-On Reality)

  • The Role: A deeply constrained, literal automation script running locally on the workspace.
  • The Mechanism: It has zero architectural autonomy and does not improvise. It reads local files, applies the exact modifications dictated by the Planner, runs the compilation or test suite, and captures the raw stdout/stderr output to feed right back up to the Planner.

Mitigating the Hazard: The Sandbox Firewall

Allowing an autonomous model to execute arbitrary shell commands on a host machine is dangerous. A single recursive directory deletion or a malformed script execution can corrupt an entire local setup.

To safely implement a hands-on executor, modern tooling enforces strict isolation boundaries:

  • Containerized Execution: The Executor agent must be isolated inside an ephemeral Docker container or a localized microVM that only mounts the specific project workspace directory. If the agent runs a catastrophic command, it merely destroys a temporary container.
  • Deterministic Tool Scoping: Do not give the local worker an open-ended terminal shell. Instead, expose a rigid, programmatic API: read_file(), patch_file(), and run_test_command().
  • The Automated Verification Gate: The loop is completely objective. The Executor continuously runs the test suite or build command inside the sandbox, iterating with the Planner until the process exits cleanly with a code 0.

The Developer's Shifted Role: This setup removes the human from the intermediate debugging rabbit hole entirely. The developer provides the high-level intent at the beginning, lets the automated loop handle the error-correction cycle in isolation, and reviews a clean, compiling Git diff at the end.

turns.response_html:
The reality of fast-paced ecosystems means that when a dependency pushes a daily patch for a security vulnerability, it frequently deprecates old syntax or alters an API contract to seal a loophole.

  • The Static Knowledge Trap: A standard model's internal weights are frozen at its training cutoff. It cannot inherently know a package changed its syntax yesterday morning to fix a CVE.
  • The Hallucination Loop: If the model guesses based on outdated documentation, the local terminal throws an error. If that error is fed back to the same conversational interface without refreshing reality, the model routinely improvises a synthetic fix that does not exist, digging the rabbit hole deeper.

To stop relying on frozen documentation, a split-agent system treats the local environment as the source of truth. Instead of letting the AI guess what works, it queries the machine directly.

The Solution: Local Runtime Grounding

An open standard designed for this type of system is the Model Context Protocol (MCP). MCP acts as a universal connector between an LLM and local tools (filesystems, development environments, and shells). By pairing a local LLM runner with an isolated sandbox via MCP, the environment can correct the model's outdated assumptions in real time.

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     LOCAL HOST MACHINE                      |
|                                                             |
|   +-------------------+         +-----------------------+   |
|   |   Planner AI      | <-----> |   Model Context       |   |
|   |   (Local LLM)     |         |   Protocol (MCP)      |   |
|   +-------------------+         +-----------------------+   |
|             ^                               ^               |
|             | (Instructions)                | (Tool Calls)  |
|             v                               v               |
|   +-----------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |               DOCKER SANDBOX CONTAINER              |   |
|   |                                                     |   |
|   |  +------------------+         +------------------+  |   |
|   |  |  Executor Agent  | <-----> |  Your Project    |  |   |
|   |  |  (CLI/Shell)     |         |  Workspace       |  |   |
|   |  +------------------+         +------------------+  |   |
|   +-----------------------------------------------------+   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Here is exactly how this procedural loop functions to bypass frozen documentation and handle real-world terminal updates:

Implementation Layer

To implement this without risking the integrity of the host machine, the setup relies on three distinct layers:

  1. The Sandbox Layer: A container engine (like Docker) that handles file isolation. The workspace directory is mounted as a volume, ensuring any catastrophic command execution or erratic shell behavior merely destroys a temporary container without impacting the main system.
  2. The Intelligence Layer: Highly capable, open-weight coding models (such as qwen3-coder:30b or reasoning-focused local variants) running on local hardware via frameworks like Ollama. These models are heavily optimized for structured tool use, file patching, and handling multi-turn terminal failures.
  3. The Protocol Layer: An MCP server running filesystem and terminal adapters. This restricts the agent to explicit APIs like read_file, patch_file, and run_command rather than leaving an unmonitored, raw shell exposed.

This workflow takes the developer out of the intermediate debugging cycle entirely. The system loops autonomously until the compiler or test framework returns a clean exit code, delivering a final, verified Git diff for review.

turns.response_html:
Introducing a third specialized role completes the triad perfectly. In advanced multi-agent workflows, this is known as the Librarian Agent (or Context Retrieval Agent).

By separating documentation retrieval from both planning and execution, the system eliminates the primary driver of the hallucination loop: the model guessing an API's signature because it lacks a local source of truth.

The Three-Agent Loop

Adding the Librarian transforms a linear guess-and-check process into a highly structured, version-anchored lifecycle:

                  +-----------------------+
                  |      1. PLANNER       |
                  |   (Abstract Logic)    |
                  +-----------------------+
                    ^                   |
    3. Exact Docs   |                   | 2. Strategy &
    & Type Specs    |                   |    Code Patches
                    |                   v
          +-------------------+   +-------------------+
          |   3. LIBRARIAN    |   |    2. EXECUTOR    |
          | (Targeted Fetch)  |   | (Local Sandbox)   |
          +-------------------+   +-------------------+
                    ^                   |
                    |                   | 1. System Versions
                    +-------------------+    & Raw Errors

This updated workflow operates via an explicit sequence:

  • The Executor Pinpoints the Target: Instead of guessing the system state, the Executor reads the environment manifests (e.g., package.json, requirements.txt, or local CLI --version flags) and outputs: "We are running dependency-xyz strictly at version v2.4.1, and the terminal error is TypeError: undefined is not a function at line 12."
  • The Librarian Fetches the Source of Truth: The Librarian takes that exact version string (v2.4.1) and retrieves the precise technical manual or type definitions for only that version. It completely ignores newer or older document variants.
  • The Planner Synthesizes the Fix: Armed with the exact error log from the Executor and the explicit version manual from the Librarian, the Planner writes a deterministic patch. It no longer has room to hallucinate syntax that doesn't exist in that specific release.

The Modern AI-Doc Standard: Bypassing the Web Scraping Trap

For a Librarian agent to work efficiently, it cannot simply browse standard consumer webpages. Scraping heavy HTML, dealing with cookie banners, and parsing client-side JavaScript consumes massive amounts of token overhead and introduces formatting noise.

Modern developer ecosystems handle this problem using two primary technologies:

1. The llms.txt Standard

An industry-wide standardization format has emerged where documentation sites host a plain-text, markdown-optimized index specifically at the root directory: /llms.txt (and a comprehensive version at /llms-full.txt).

  • The Advantage: These files strip out all visual chrome, CSS, and navigation sidebars, serving dense, machine-readable markdown.
  • Version Pinning: A robust Librarian agent targets the versioned path of these files (e.g., [docs.example.com/v2.4.1/llms.txt](https://docs.example.com/v2.4.1/llms.txt)) to ingest a complete, unpolluted map of parameters, error schemas, and breaking changes in a single request.

2. Documentation MCP Servers

Under the Model Context Protocol (MCP), open-source and platform-specific documentation servers (such as specialized doc indexers) wrap documentation APIs into uniform tool definitions. Rather than treating documentation as a web-search problem, the Librarian calls deterministic tools like search_documentation(package="xyz", version="2.4.1", query="auth") to receive structured JSON objects containing exact API contracts.

Why this prevents the rabbit hole: When security patches alter terminal tools or code syntax daily, the local system configuration changes. By forcing the Librarian to fetch documentation mapped exclusively to the local environment's current package versions, the Planner agent is always grounded in the absolute reality of the host machine.
